newsitem.title: DUBAI: Qatar emir determined to hold Mideast summit.
newsitem.headline: Qatar emir determined to hold Mideast summit.

text.p: Qatar's controversial emir appears to be on a collision course with his Arab allies over an international economic summit he is due to host later this year.

Emir Sheikh Hamad bin Khalifa al-Thani said in remarks published over the weekend he was determined to convene the showpiece Middle East and North Africa economic meeting (MENA) in his capital Doha in November.
"We are determined to live up to our international obligations with regard to convening the economic conference in Doha," Sheikh Hamad told Kuwaiti daily newspaper al-Rai al-Aam.
Israel traditionally attends the annual summit, which was launched in 1994 and was held last year in Egypt.
Some Arab states have threatened to boycott the Doha summit over the deadlocked Middle East peace process.

U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, on her first visit to the Middle East, will head Washington's delegation to Qatar, whose vast energy resources and small population give it one of the world's highest gross national products per capita.
The United States, in remarks aimed at its close ally Saudi Arabia, has encouraged all Arab countries to take part in the gathering.

But some Arab states, including regional powerhouse Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE), have said they would stay away if there was no progress in deadlocked peace talks between Israel and the Palestinians.
The Saudis have urged Qatar to cancel the summit, which would be the first session of the event to be held in the strategic Gulf region.

Jordan said it would attend only if other Arab states did so, and other key Arab states including Egypt and Morocco have said they would wait to see whether there was any progress in the stalled peace process.
Syria, Lebanon, Iraq and Libya have not attended any of the three previous MENA summits. Syria has urged Arab states to boycott this year's event.

The Arab League's assistant secretary-general Abdel-Rahman al-Sihibani, said last week Qatar might cancel the summit unless Israel changed its policy of building Jewish settlements in Arab East Jerusalem, earmarked by the Palestinians as capital of a future state of Palestine.
But Washington's desire for a successful meeting in Doha was likely to be persuasive, Gulf analysts said on Sunday.

"It will go ahead," one analyst said. "It is very difficult for the Saudis and the Egyptians to defy the West. France has declared it will attend, Britain is also participating, and the United States has said outright it will be there."
It is not the first time Sheikh Hamad has been at odds with Qatar's Arab allies.

Six months after seizing power from his father in a bloodless palace coup two years ago he walked out of a Gulf Arab summit, infuriating Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, the UAE, Bahrain and host Oman, over the appointment of a Saudi to head the six-nation Gulf Cooperation Council.
